Q1. Discuss the major goals of AI - perception, reasoning, planning, communication,
creativity, learning, and control/manipulation - and explain how Generative AI is
contributing to these goals.
Answer. Artificial Intelligence aims to build systems that can perceive the world, form useful
internal representations, reason about alternatives, act toward goals, communicate with humans,
learn from experience, and manipulate digital or physical environments. Generative AI contributes
strongly because it learns data distributions and can produce new content rather than only assigning
labels.
1. Perception: Perception is the ability to interpret inputs such as images, audio, video, text, and
sensor measurements. Generative models can learn rich representations of such inputs and can
reconstruct, synthesize, denoise, complete, or transform them. For example, a diffusion model
can learn the visual structure of images and then generate an image from a text description.
2. Reasoning: Reasoning requires forming relationships among facts and drawing conclusions.
Large generative models can represent patterns from large corpora and generate intermediate
explanations, hypotheses, or candidate solutions. In practical systems, generation is often
combined with retrieval, tools, search, or symbolic checks so that the generated reasoning is
grounded in external evidence.
3. Planning: Planning means selecting a sequence of actions that moves a system from an initial
state to a desired goal. Generative models can propose candidate action sequences, simulate
possible outcomes, or generate sub-goals. The generated plan can then be verified by a planner,
simulator, or constraint checker.
4. Communication: Generative models naturally support language generation, translation,
summarization, dialogue, question answering, and multimodal interaction. This allows a machine
to communicate information in a form suitable for a human or another agent.
5. Creativity: Generative AI can synthesize novel text, images, music, video, 3D assets, software
code, and design candidates. The key point is that the output is newly generated from learned
statistical structure rather than simply retrieved as an exact stored example.
6. Learning: Generative models learn a representation of the underlying data distribution.
Learning may be supervised, weakly supervised, or unsupervised. Latent-variable models are
especially useful because they can discover hidden factors of variation and provide compact
representations.
7. Control and manipulation: A generative model can serve as a simulator or world model,
predicting plausible future states and helping an agent choose actions. In robotics, for example,
a model can generate predicted observations under candidate actions. The actual control loop
still requires feedback and safety constraints.
Overall, Generative AI expands AI from classification and prediction toward synthesis and simulation.
It is therefore useful as a component of systems that perceive, reason, plan, communicate, create,
learn, and act.
Exam Tip
In an exam, connect each AI goal to one clear generative capability and one concrete application.
This makes the answer both conceptual and application-oriented.

Q2. Explain the major capabilities of Generative AI with its major applications.
Explain how the scaling of Generative AI models depends on data, model parameters,
computational resources, memory, and distributed training. Discuss why scaling
becomes increasingly challenging as model size increases.
Answer. Generative AI learns a probability distribution over data and can then sample or condition
the learned distribution to create new outputs. Its major capabilities include text generation, image
generation, audio/music synthesis, video generation, code generation, multimodal generation, data
augmentation, completion, inpainting, style transfer, and simulation.
• Text: writing, summarization, translation, tutoring, question answering, code generation.
• Images: text-to-image, image completion, editing, super-resolution, synthetic data generation.
• Audio and music: speech synthesis, voice conversion, music generation, sound effects.
• Video: text-to-video, video continuation, editing, avatar generation.
• Multimodal: generating or transforming combinations of text, images, audio, and video.
• Scientific/engineering uses: molecular design, synthetic datasets, simulation, inverse design,
and reconstruction.
Scaling depends on several interacting resources:
• Data scale: Larger models generally need more diverse, high-quality data. Insufficient or
repetitive data limits generalization and can increase overfitting or memorization.
• Model parameters: Increasing parameters increases representational capacity. More parame￾ters allow the model to represent more complex functions, but also increase training and inference
cost.
• Compute: Training requires matrix operations over many examples and many optimization
steps. Compute therefore grows with model size, data size, sequence length, and number of
training steps.
• Memory: Parameters, optimizer states, activations, gradients, and temporary buffers must be
stored. Optimizer state can require several times the memory of the parameter tensors.
• Distributed training: Large models are split across multiple accelerators using data parallelism,
tensor/model parallelism, or pipeline parallelism. Communication and synchronization become
major system costs.
Why scaling gets harder: Memory pressure grows because parameters and training states may no
longer fit on one device. Communication overhead grows as devices exchange activations, gradients,
or parameters. Training becomes more sensitive to data quality, optimization stability, and numerical
precision. Inference also becomes expensive because every generated token or output sample may
require many large matrix operations. The practical bottleneck shifts from pure arithmetic to the
complete system: memory bandwidth, network bandwidth, synchronization, storage, and reliability.
Exam Tip
Remember the central idea: scaling is not only about buying a larger model. Data, parameters,
compute, memory, and communication must scale together.

Q4. Explain the major challenges in deep generative modeling, particularly for high￾dimensional data such as images. Explain how these challenges affect the ability to
generate realistic samples and perform discriminative tasks.
Answer. High-dimensional data create a very large sample space. A 64 x 64 RGB image already has
64 x 64 x 3 pixel values; the number of possible images is enormous. Learning a useful distribution
over that space is therefore much harder than learning a distribution over a small set of scalar
variables.
• Curse of dimensionality: Data become sparse in high-dimensional space, so enormous amounts
of training data may be needed.
• Complex dependencies: Pixels are not independent; edges, shapes, textures, object parts,
lighting, and semantics interact across many spatial scales.
• Likelihood difficulty: Exact likelihoods may be hard or expensive to compute for complex
models.
• Optimization difficulty: Deep non-convex objectives can have unstable gradients and sensitive
hyperparameters.
• Mode coverage: A model may generate sharp samples but miss important modes of the real
distribution, or generate diverse outputs that lack realism.
• Representation quality: A poor latent representation can hurt interpolation, controllability,
and downstream classification.
These challenges affect generation because unrealistic or repeated samples appear when the learned
distribution is poor. They affect discrimination because a generative representation may fail to
preserve class-relevant factors. Conversely, a well-learned generative representation can provide
useful features for classification, clustering, semi-supervised learning, or retrieval.

Q8. Medical diagnosis: Cancer C1 has prior 0.10 and likelihood 0.80; No Cancer C2 has
prior 0.90 and likelihood 0.20. Using Bayes theorem, calculate posterior probabilities
and classify the X-ray.
Answer. Let the observed X-ray result be x. The unnormalized joint probabilities are p(x, C1) =
0.10 × 0.80 = 0.08 and p(x, C2) = 0.90 × 0.20 = 0.18.
p(x) = 0.08 + 0.18 = 0.26
p(C1 | x) = 0.08
0.26
≈ 0.3077 ≈ 30.77%
p(C2 | x) = 0.18
0.26
≈ 0.6923 ≈ 69.23%
The posterior probability is therefore larger for C2 (No Cancer). Under the usual maximum-posterior
classification rule, the observation is classified as No Cancer.
Roles of the terms:
• Prior = initial prevalence/belief before observing the X-ray.
• Likelihood = compatibility of the observed X-ray result with each class.
• Posterior = updated probability after seeing the observation.
• Normalization constant = p(x)=0.26, which converts the unnormalized values 0.08 and 0.18
into probabilities that sum to 1.
Exam Tip
The important exam point is that a high likelihood for a class does not automatically make
that class the final decision. The prior also matters.

Answer. A generative model learns a mapping between latent variables and data space. Studying
that mapping helps determine whether the model has learned meaningful structure.

the learned generator can map ordinary latent points to realistic data. Example: sample several

change smoothly, the latent space contains meaningful continuous structure.
z(α) = (1 − α)z1 + αz2, 0 ≤ α ≤ 1

semantic factors such as pose, hair color, or lighting. Example: changing one latent direction
may alter head pose while leaving identity mostly unchanged. This makes the representation
more interpretable and controllable.

Q1. Explain the motivation for using latent variable models. For the image example,
answer (a)-(d).
Answer. Latent variable models introduce hidden variables z that explain underlying structure in
observed data x. This is useful because high-dimensional observations often arise from a smaller

ideal disentangled representation, changing one factor would have a focused semantic effect. (c)

generated. This conditional problem can be simpler because z summarizes the important causes.

image. Learning or approximating this posterior provides an unsupervised representation of the
data. The latent vector can then be used for clustering, visualization, interpolation, reconstruction,
or downstream tasks.

Q1. Explain the architecture and working principle of a GAN. Describe G and D, the
minimax game, and the objective function.
Answer. A Generative Adversarial Network consists of two neural networks: a generator Gθ
and a discriminator Dϕ. The generator maps a random latent vector z into a synthetic sample
G(z). The discriminator receives either a real sample x from the data distribution or a generated
sample and outputs a probability that the input is real. Training alternates between two goals. The
discriminator learns to assign high probability to real data and low probability to generated data.
The generator learns to produce samples that the discriminator classifies as real.
V (D, G) = Ex∼pdata [log D(x)] + Ez∼p(z)

The minimax game is minG maxD V (D, G):
• First term: rewards D for correctly recognizing real samples.
• Second term: rewards D for correctly rejecting generated samples.
D maximizes the objective because it wants accurate discrimination. G minimizes it in the original
minimax formulation because it wants the discriminator to fail on generated samples. In practical
implementations, the non-saturating generator loss −Ez[log D(G(z))] is often used because it gives
stronger gradients early in training.

Q5. Discuss major practical GAN training challenges, including unstable optimization
and mode collapse. Explain oscillating losses and empirical mitigation approaches.
Answer. GAN training is a two-player game rather than an ordinary single-objective optimization
problem. The generator and discriminator continually adapt to one another, so the target seen by
one network changes as the other is updated.
• Unstable optimization: If D becomes too strong, G may receive weak or unhelpful gradients
in some formulations. If G improves too quickly, D can become inaccurate. The balance can
therefore oscillate rather than converge smoothly.
• Oscillating losses: GAN losses need not decrease monotonically. A decrease in discriminator
loss can make generator loss increase and vice versa. Moreover, the numerical value of a GAN
loss depends on the current opponent, so it is not a standalone quality score.
• Mode collapse: The generator maps many different latent vectors to similar outputs. The
samples may look realistic but fail to cover the diversity of the real data distribution. Example:
a face generator repeatedly produces faces with very similar pose, hairstyle, and background
while ignoring other valid variations.
• Empirical mitigation: commonly used approaches include improved discriminator regulariza￾tion, careful learning-rate/β tuning, minibatch-based diversity mechanisms, feature matching,
alternative adversarial objectives, spectral normalization, gradient penalties, data augmentation,
and architectural changes. No single method guarantees complete elimination of collapse.
31

Q7. Explain why evaluating generative models is challenging and how evaluation
depends on the intended task. Cover density estimation, sampling, latent representation
learning, and downstream applications.
Answer. No single evaluation score captures all aspects of a generative model. A model may have
good likelihood but produce visually weak samples, or produce visually impressive samples while
missing modes of the true distribution. Evaluation must therefore match the intended use.
• Density estimation: Evaluate likelihood or held-out log-likelihood when the model explicitly
provides a tractable or comparable density. The goal is whether the learned probability model
assigns appropriate probability to unseen data.
• Sampling/generation: Evaluate realism, diversity, fidelity, coverage, and human or task￾specific quality. Image metrics such as IS and FID are common, but they are imperfect proxies.
• Latent representation learning: Evaluate whether latent codes capture meaningful factors,
support smooth interpolation, clustering, reconstruction, or disentanglement.
• Downstream applications: Evaluate the actual task, such as semi-supervised classification,
image translation, retrieval, completion, augmentation, or domain adaptation. The generated
data or latent representation should improve the target application rather than only score well
on a generic metric.
33

Q8. Explain the Inception Score (IS). Discuss high sharpness and high diversity using

each generated sample x, c(y|x) is the classifier prediction over labels. A high-quality image should
produce a confident prediction, so c(y|x) has low entropy. Across many generated images, the
marginal c(y)=E_x[c(y|x)] should have high entropy so that the generator covers many classes.

measurement of pixel-level realism and depends on the chosen classifier.

Q1. Explain the architecture and working principle of a Conditional GAN (cGAN).
How does conditioning on class information modify a conventional GAN? Explain
text-to-image use.
Answer. A conditional GAN adds an observed condition y, such as a class label or text description,
to both the generator and discriminator. Instead of learning G(z), the generator learns G(z,y), while
the discriminator evaluates whether a sample is real and whether it is consistent with y.
V (D, G) = Ex,y∼pdata [log D(x, y)] + Ez∼p(z), y∼p(y)
[log(1 − D(G(z, y), y))]
For class-conditional image generation, y could be the label “cat” or “car”. The generator receives z
and y and creates an image matching the requested class. For text-to-image synthesis, y is replaced
by a learned text embedding; the generator uses that embedding as semantic conditioning and D
checks image-text compatibility as part of its discrimination task.

Q2. Explain the motivation behind BiGAN. Describe how G and E learn the joint
distributions of (X,Z), and state the inverse-mapping condition.
Answer. A conventional GAN learns to map z to x but does not naturally provide the inverse
mapping from an observed x back to a latent z. A Bidirectional GAN (BiGAN) introduces an
encoder E(x) to infer a latent representation from real data. The discriminator receives pairs rather
than single samples. From the generator path it sees (z,G(z)). From the encoder path it sees
(E(x),x). The discriminator learns to distinguish these two joint distributions, while G and E learn
together to make them indistinguishable.
• Joint 1 (generator path): (z, G(z))
• Joint 2 (encoder path): (E(x), x)
When training is successful and the mappings are compatible, E and G become approximately
inverse on the data manifold: E(G(z)) ≈ z and G(E(x)) ≈ x for relevant samples. BiGAN therefore
supports both sample generation and latent inference.

Q3. CoGAN for two semantically related but unpaired domains X_A and X_B: explain
learning without correspondence supervision, weight sharing, and one limitation.
Answer. CoGAN uses two GAN-style networks, one per domain, and couples them through shared
parameters. The domains may contain related semantic objects but there are no paired examples
saying which image in A corresponds to which image in B. The domain-specific parts capture
low-level appearance differences, while shared layers encourage the two networks to encode common
high-level semantics. Because shared parameters are trained from both domains, the model can
learn a common latent structure without explicit image-to-image correspondences. Weight sharing
is an inductive bias: if high-level concepts such as “object category” are common across domains,
sharing deeper layers encourages the networks to discover representations useful to both. Earlier
layers are often left separate because low-level statistics such as color, texture, and contrast may
differ by domain. Limitation: CoGAN relies on the assumption that the two domains share useful
high-level semantics. If their underlying structures differ strongly, the shared representation may be
inappropriate; training can also be sensitive to the domain gap and adversarial optimization.
39

It contains two generators and two discriminators: G : X → Y , F : Y → X, D_Y distinguishes real
Y from G(X), and D_X distinguishes real X from F(Y). Adversarial loss in the X->Y direction
encourages G(x) to look like a real Y image. A second adversarial loss does the analogous job for
F(y) in the Y->X direction.
Ladv(G, DY , X, Y ) = Ey[log DY (y)] + Ex[log(1 − DY (G(x)))]
Cycle consistency requires that translating to the other domain and back approximately reproduces
the input: F(G(x)) ≈ x, G(F(y)) ≈ y

an image from Y is passed through G and should remain close to itself. Cycle consistency alone
does not uniquely determine the intended semantic mapping: multiple mappings can satisfy the
cycle constraint, including undesirable ones. Adversarial, identity, and architectural biases therefore
work together.

Q6. Explain BiGAN motivation, compare with conventional GAN, roles of G/E/D,

Answer. The key addition in BiGAN is an encoder E that maps observed data to latent space. A
conventional GAN has G:z->x but no explicit learned inverse x->z. BiGAN learns both directions
through a joint adversarial game. G: generates x from z. E: maps x to a latent representation z_hat.
D: distinguishes joint pairs (z,G(z)) from (E(x),x). The discriminator never needs to decide whether
z or x is individually real. Instead, it checks whether the pair has been produced by the generator
side or the encoder/data side. When the joint distributions match, the encoder and generator are
approximately inverse on the relevant manifolds. After training, generation is performed by sampling
z and computing G(z). Representation inference is performed by taking a real x and computing
E(x). This makes BiGAN useful when both synthesis and latent embeddings are required.

Q7. Explain the problem of image-to-image translation X<->Y without paired exam￾ples. Describe CycleGAN architecture and adversarial training in both directions.

because the correct y_i paired with x_i is unknown. CycleGAN addresses this by learning two
mappings: G : X → Y and F : Y → X, with discriminators D_Y and D_X. For G : X → Y , D_Y

match the distribution of Y. For F : Y → X, D_X sees real x samples and generated F(y) samples.
The adversarial objective encourages F(y) to match the distribution of X. The cycle losses link the
two directions so that the learned mapping preserves information relevant to the original sample
rather than producing arbitrary samples from the target domain.

do not supply a direct ground-truth target.
LGAN(G, DY , X, Y ) = Ey[log DY (y)] + Ex[log(1 − DY (G(x)))]
LGAN(F, DX, Y, X) = Ex[log DX(x)] + Ey[log(1 − DX(F(y)))]
Lcyc(G, F) = Ex[∥F(G(x)) − x∥1] + Ey[∥G(F(y)) − y∥1]
LCycleGAN = LGAN(G, DY , X, Y ) + LGAN(F, DX, Y, X) + λLcyc(G, F)
The two adversarial terms make translated samples look realistic in their respective target domains.
The cycle term prevents the mappings from ignoring the input structure. Lambda controls the
trade-off: a larger λ places more emphasis on reconstruction through the cycle, while a smaller λ
gives relatively greater weight to adversarial realism. Some implementations add an identity term
as a further regularizer, but the complete objective requested in the source explicitly centers on the
two adversarial losses plus the λ-weighted cycle loss.

Q1. How does a Convolutional VAE address the curse of dimensionality? Illustrate
the architecture.
Answer. A fully connected layer applied directly to a high-resolution image treats every input
pixel as an independent input to every output neuron. This creates a huge parameter count and
ignores local spatial structure. A convolutional VAE replaces the early fully connected processing
with convolutional layers that use local receptive fields and shared weights. Typical architecture:
Input image ⇒ Conv + activation ⇒ Conv + activation
⇓
latent parameter heads (µ, log σ
2
) ⇒ reparameterization
⇓
decoder ⇒ Transposed Conv / Upsampling + Conv ⇒ reconstructed image
• Local connectivity: each filter sees a small neighborhood.
• Weight sharing: the same filter is reused across the image, sharply reducing parameters.
• Hierarchical features: early layers learn edges/ textures; deeper layers learn larger shapes
and semantic structures.
Spatial structure is preserved through feature maps rather than immediately flattening the image.
Thus, the convolutional encoder makes high-dimensional image modeling more parameter-efficient
and statistically appropriate. The decoder reverses this hierarchy to reconstruct the image.

Q2. Explain the architecture and objective of a Conditional VAE (CVAE). How does
conditioning influence the latent representation and generated output?
Answer. A CVAE introduces an observed conditioning variable y such as a class label, attribute,
or text embedding. The encoder models qϕ(z | x, y), the decoder models pθ(x | z, y), and the prior
can also be conditioned when appropriate.
LCVAE = Eqϕ
[− log pθ(x | z, y)] + DKL(qϕ(z | x, y)∥p(z | y))
The condition tells the encoder what context must be explained and tells the decoder what kind
of sample to generate. For example, with y=“digit 7”, the decoder can generate an image that
resembles a 7 while z captures the remaining variation such as stroke width or style. Conditioning
therefore makes generation controllable rather than purely random with respect to the target
attribute.
47

Q3. Explain β-VAE, write the modified objective, explain β, and discuss disentangle￾ment.
Answer. Beta-VAE modifies the standard VAE by multiplying the KL divergence term by a
hyperparameter β. The standard VAE balances reconstruction and latent regularization with weight
1. Beta-VAE changes this trade-off.
Lβ-VAE = Eqϕ
[− log pθ(x | z)] + βDKL(qϕ(z | x)∥p(z))
When β = 1, this is the standard VAE objective. For β > 1, the KL term is emphasized more
strongly. This limits the amount of information that can pass through the latent code and encourages
the latent variables to conform more closely to the factorized prior N (0, I). Because the prior
factorizes and the KL pressure discourages arbitrary correlations and excessive information, β-VAE
often encourages disentangled factors. However, stronger regularization can increase reconstruction
error or remove fine-grained information. Therefore β controls an information-capacity trade-off
rather than guaranteeing perfect disentanglement.
48

Q4. Explain the motivation for Ladder VAE (LVAE). How does it learn a hierarchical
latent representation? Compare conventional hierarchical VAE and ladder architecture.
Answer. A Ladder VAE is motivated by the observation that real data often have hierarchical
structure: low-level details such as edges may depend on medium-level shapes, which in turn
depend on high-level concepts. A single latent layer may not represent this hierarchy efficiently. A
hierarchical VAE may contain multiple latent variables z1,z2,. . . at different abstraction levels. In a
conventional arrangement, the encoder processes information upward while the decoder samples
latents downward. The ladder architecture adds top-down and bottom-up pathways so that
information at corresponding levels can be combined, allowing each latent variable to be refined
using both inference evidence and generative context. Conceptual flow: x -> bottom-up features
-> z1 -> z2 -> z3 (high-level) Top-down path: z3 -> z2 -> z1 -> reconstruction The advantage
is hierarchical representation: higher latents can capture broad semantic factors, while lower
latents preserve local detail. Ladder structures also help inference networks combine bottom-up
evidence with top-down priors, improving the modeling of hierarchical uncertainty.
49

Q5. β-VAE reconstruction loss = 18.5 and KL loss = 2.4. Objective = L_reconstruction
+ β L_KL. Calculate for β=1,2,4 and explain the effect of increasing β.
Answer. Use L = 18.5 + β(2.4).
β = 1 : L = 18.5 + 2.4 = 20.9
β = 2 : L = 18.5 + 4.8 = 23.3
β = 4 : L = 18.5 + 9.6 = 28.1
As β increases, the KL divergence receives more weight relative to reconstruction. The model is
pushed harder toward the prior N (0, I), which reduces the effective information capacity of the
latent channel and can encourage a more structured/disentangled representation. The trade-off is
that reconstruction can become less accurate because less information is allowed to be encoded in z.
